title: Oral cancer: signs, risks & urgent referral
blurb: The risk factors, red flags and high-risk sites of mouth cancer, and why a painless ulcer lasting more than three weeks must never be ignored.
question: During a check-up, the dentist looks closely at a painless ulcer on the side of a patient's tongue. The patient, a 58-year-old who smokes and drinks most evenings, says it has been there 'about a month' but doesn't bother him. What does this suggest, and what should happen next?

teach.body: Oral (mouth) cancer can affect the tongue, floor of the mouth, cheeks, gums, palate and lips. Most are squamous cell carcinomas, which start in the lining of the mouth. Found early, treatment is simpler and survival far better, but many cases are found late because early cancer is usually painless. The dentist checks the soft tissues at every examination, so the dental team is often first to spot it. Your role: record findings, notice changes, take the concern seriously and alert the dentist. Dental nurses do not diagnose.

teach.h: What a suspicious lesion can look like
teach.caption: An irregular ulcer on the side of the tongue, with a mixed red and white surface and a raised, thickened edge. A lesion like this needs urgent referral, whether or not it hurts.

head: Red flag
What you might see or hear
rows: Not healing, even after any cause is removed
Velvety red (erythroplakia) or speckled red and white (erythroleukoplakia)
Won't rub off (leukoplakia): potentially malignant, needs the dentist's assessment
Feels firm (induration); rolled or irregular edge
Persistent swelling of a lymph node
Numbness, unexplained loose teeth, pain on swallowing or hoarseness lasting over 3 weeks
teach.caption: No single feature proves cancer, and only a biopsy can confirm it. Any red flag means the dentist must see it now.

teach.h: Why smoking and drinking together are worse
teach.caption: Alcohol helps tobacco's carcinogens soak into the lining of the mouth, so the two risks multiply each other.

rows.label: Smokeless tobacco, betel quid, paan, gutka, areca nut
Diet low in fruit and vegetables
Older age, male sex, weakened immunity

teach.note: Betel quid and areca nut chewing is common in some South Asian communities. Ask about it directly and record it in the social history.

teach.body: The highest-risk sites inside the mouth are the lateral (side) borders and underside of the tongue and the floor of the mouth, where saliva pools carcinogens. The lower lip is the classic site for sun-related lip cancer. HPV-related cancers mainly affect the oropharynx: the tonsils, soft palate and base of the tongue, sometimes in younger non-smokers. The dentist also feels the neck for lymph nodes, because oral cancer spreads there first.

steps.label: Dysplasia
steps.sub: Abnormal cells; may show as a red or white patch

steps.label: Carcinoma in situ
steps.sub: Cancer cells still confined to the surface layer

steps.label: Invasive cancer
steps.sub: Breaks into deeper tissue; can spread to neck nodes

teach.caption: Risk factors such as tobacco and alcohol push cells along this path over years. Catching it at the patch stage is the goal.

teach.h: What you do if you spot something

steps.label: Take it seriously
steps.sub: Never dismiss it, and never diagnose it yourself

steps.label: Tell the dentist now
steps.sub: Before the patient leaves the chair

steps.label: Record accurately
steps.sub: Site, size, colour, how long it's been there; photo if practice policy allows

steps.label: Urgent referral
steps.sub: Dentist refers on the urgent suspected cancer pathway (often called the 'two-week wait')

steps.label: Follow up
steps.sub: Check the referral was sent and the patient attended

teach.text: No pain does not mean no problem. Early oral cancer is usually painless, which is exactly why patients ignore it. Never reassure a patient that a lesion is 'nothing' or suggest waiting to see if it clears.

items: Red flags: ulcer over 3 weeks, red or white patches, hard lump or rolled edge, neck lump.
Main risks: tobacco and alcohol (multiplied together), betel/areca, HPV, sun for the lip.
High-risk sites: side and underside of the tongue, floor of the mouth.
Path: healthy → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive cancer.
Action: record, alert the dentist immediately, dentist makes an urgent suspected-cancer referral, follow up.

summary: You can now list the main risk factors for oral cancer and explain why tobacco and alcohol together are so dangerous, recognise the red flags and high-risk sites, describe how cancer develops from dysplasia, and set out exactly what you do when a suspicious lesion is found: record it, alert the dentist at once and make sure the urgent referral happens.

A.q: A patient attends with an ulcer on the side of the tongue that has been present for over three weeks and has not improved. What is the most appropriate action by the dental team?
options: Review it again in six weeks' time
Prescribe a mouthwash and reassure
Record it and arrange urgent referral
Advise a salt-water rinse for a month
A.why: An ulcer lasting more than three weeks is a red flag. It must be recorded and the dentist should refer urgently on the suspected cancer pathway.

whyNot.0: Waiting another six weeks delays diagnosis of a possible cancer.
whyNot.1: A mouthwash and reassurance could mask a serious lesion and delay referral.
whyNot.3: Home remedies are not appropriate once an ulcer has lasted over three weeks.

A.q: A patient's social history is being recorded before an oral cancer check. Which combination of habits most increases the risk of oral cancer?
options: Smoking and heavy drinking
Vaping and fizzy drinks
Sugary snacks and coffee
Nail biting and teeth grinding
A.why: Tobacco and alcohol are the two main risk factors, and together they multiply each other's effect.

whyNot.1: Fizzy drinks are linked to erosion, not oral cancer, and vaping is not the classic combined risk.
whyNot.2: Sugar and coffee affect caries and staining, not oral cancer risk.
whyNot.3: Nail biting and grinding cause tooth wear, not cancer.

A.q: Which part of the mouth is a high-risk site for oral cancer?
options: The midline of the hard palate
The gum around the upper incisors
The tip of the tongue's top surface
The floor of the mouth
A.why: The floor of the mouth, with the side and underside of the tongue, is among the highest-risk sites, partly because saliva carrying carcinogens pools there.

whyNot.0: The hard palate can be affected but is not one of the highest-risk sites.
whyNot.1: The gingiva around upper incisors is not a classic high-risk site.
whyNot.2: It is the lateral border and underside of the tongue, not the top of the tip, that is high risk.

B.q: A trainee nurse is learning which lesions need urgent referral. Which description is a red flag for oral cancer?
options: A white coating that wipes off easily
An ulcer with a hard, rolled edge
A cheek bite that healed in ten days
A cold sore that crusted within a week
B.why: Induration (hardness) and a raised, rolled or irregular edge are classic warning features of a malignant ulcer.

whyNot.0: A white coating that wipes off is typical of thrush (candidosis).
whyNot.2: A traumatic ulcer that healed once the cause stopped is reassuring.
whyNot.3: Cold sores are viral and heal within about 10 days.

B.q: A patient who smokes asks why it raises his risk of mouth cancer. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Smoke dries the mouth and causes decay
Smoke heats the mouth and kills nerves
Smoke stains the teeth and gums brown
Chemicals in smoke damage cells' DNA
B.why: Tobacco contains carcinogens that damage the DNA of cells lining the mouth, which can lead to dysplasia and cancer.

whyNot.0: Dry mouth increases caries risk, but this is not why smoking causes cancer.
whyNot.1: Heat is not the main mechanism; the carcinogens are.
whyNot.2: Staining is a cosmetic effect and does not cause cancer.

B.q: Which sequence correctly describes how oral cancer develops?
options: Healthy → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ → invasive
Healthy → invasive → dysplasia → carcinoma in situ
Dysplasia → healthy → invasive → carcinoma in situ
Healthy → carcinoma in situ → invasive → dysplasia
B.why: Cells first become abnormal (dysplasia), then cancerous but confined to the surface (carcinoma in situ), then invade deeper tissue.

whyNot.1: Invasion is the final stage, not the second.
whyNot.2: Dysplasia cannot come before healthy tissue; the sequence starts with normal cells.
whyNot.3: Dysplasia comes before carcinoma in situ, not after invasion.

C.q: A patient with a lesion on the floor of the mouth says she has ignored it because it isn't painful. What is the best action for the dental nurse?
options: Reassure her that painless lesions are harmless
Make sure the dentist sees it before she leaves
Book a routine recall in six months to recheck it
Suggest she sees her GP if it becomes painful
C.why: Painless lesions can still be cancerous. The nurse should make sure it is documented and the dentist sees it immediately.

whyNot.0: Lack of pain is not reassuring; early oral cancer is often painless.
whyNot.2: A six-month wait could allow a cancer to progress.
whyNot.3: Waiting for pain would delay diagnosis, and the dentist should assess it now.

C.q: HPV infection is most strongly linked to cancer in which area?
options: The lower lip
The hard palate
The oropharynx
The attached gum
C.why: HPV-related cancers mainly affect the oropharynx, such as the tonsils and base of the tongue.

whyNot.0: Lower lip cancer is mainly linked to sun (UV) exposure.
whyNot.1: The hard palate is not the main site of HPV-related cancer.
whyNot.3: The attached gingiva is not the typical site of HPV-related cancer.

C.q: While taking a social history, a patient mentions she chews paan containing areca nut every day. How should this be treated?
options: As a harmless cultural habit
As a cause of tooth wear only
As relevant only if she smokes
As a major oral cancer risk
C.why: Betel quid, paan and areca nut are major risk factors for oral cancer and must be recorded and flagged to the dentist.

whyNot.0: It is far from harmless; it is a recognised carcinogenic habit.
whyNot.1: It can stain and wear teeth, but its main significance is cancer risk.
whyNot.2: Areca nut is a risk factor in its own right, with or without smoking.

reteach.title: The three-week rule
reteach.question: Most mouth ulcers heal by themselves within one or two weeks. So what makes the three-week mark so important?

blocks.body: A bitten cheek or a sore from a sharp tooth heals once the cause is gone, usually within a week or two. Ordinary mouth ulcers do the same. A cancer does not heal, and it often doesn't hurt. So the rule is simple: any ulcer, patch or lump that is still there after three weeks is treated as possible cancer until proven otherwise. That is not your diagnosis to make, but it IS your concern to raise.

items.label: Ulcer noticed (may be blamed on a bite)
Ordinary ulcers usually heal by now
Still there: red flag, tell the dentist
Dentist makes an urgent suspected cancer referral

blocks.caption: A non-healing ulcer on the side of the tongue. The glass is a reminder that alcohol, especially combined with smoking, is a major risk factor.

blocks.text: The patient saying 'it doesn't hurt' or 'it's just where I bit it' does not change the action. Over three weeks means the dentist must assess it now.

explain.body: Tobacco (smoked or chewed) and alcohol are the two main causes, and together they multiply the risk. Betel quid, paan and areca nut are major risks too. HPV is linked to throat-area cancers, and sun exposure to lip cancer. Recording these in the social history helps the dentist judge risk.

explain.caption: A smoker with tobacco-stained teeth and a white patch on the lower lip. Any persistent white patch needs the dentist's assessment.

test.q: Why is a patient who both smokes and drinks heavily at especially high risk?
options: Their two risks multiply each other
Alcohol cancels out the smoking risk
Only the alcohol actually matters
Smoking just stains; drinking causes it
test.why: Alcohol helps tobacco carcinogens penetrate the lining of the mouth, so the combined risk is far greater than either alone.

whyNot.1: Alcohol increases, not cancels, the effect of tobacco.
whyNot.2: Tobacco is a major risk factor in its own right.
whyNot.3: Tobacco carcinogens directly damage DNA; it is not just staining.

explain.body: Report any ulcer lasting over three weeks, red patches (erythroplakia), white or speckled patches that won't rub off (leukoplakia), hard lumps or rolled edges, and a persistent neck lump. Numbness, unexplained loose teeth and difficulty swallowing are warnings too.

test.q: Which finding is a red flag for oral cancer?
options: A soft ulcer that healed in a week
A white coating that wipes away
A red, velvety patch under the tongue
Lacy white lines that come and go
test.why: A red velvety patch (erythroplakia), especially in a high-risk site, carries a high risk of being dysplastic or malignant.

whyNot.0: An ulcer that heals quickly is reassuring.
whyNot.1: A coating that wipes off is typical of thrush.
whyNot.3: Fluctuating lacy white lines suggest lichen planus, which the dentist monitors but is not an urgent red flag in itself.

explain.body: Look hardest at the side and underside of the tongue and the floor of the mouth. The lower lip is the main site for sun-related lip cancer, and the tonsils and base of the tongue for HPV-related cancer. Cancer spreads first to the lymph nodes in the neck.

explain.caption: The lateral border of the tongue is one of the commonest sites for oral cancer.

test.q: From the sites below, which is MOST commonly affected by oral cancer?
options: The upper attached gingiva
The lateral border of the tongue
The incisal edges of the teeth
The hard palate midline
test.why: The lateral (side) border of the tongue is one of the commonest sites, along with the underside of the tongue and the floor of the mouth.

whyNot.0: The attached gingiva can be affected, but far less often than the tongue.
whyNot.2: Teeth do not develop squamous cell carcinoma; it arises in the soft-tissue lining.
whyNot.3: The hard palate is a less common site.

explain.body: Never diagnose, never dismiss. Tell the dentist straight away and record exactly what was seen. The dentist refers on the urgent suspected cancer pathway (often still called the 'two-week wait'), so the patient is fast-tracked to a specialist team. Then check the referral went and was attended.

test.q: A patient has had an unexplained ulcer for six weeks. What should the dental nurse make sure happens?
options: The patient is told to wait a few more weeks
The dentist is aware so urgent referral follows
The nurse refers the patient to hospital herself
The ulcer is treated with a steroid cream first
test.why: The nurse's role is to make sure the dentist knows so that the urgent suspected-cancer referral is made without delay.

whyNot.0: Further waiting delays possible cancer diagnosis.
whyNot.2: Referral is made by the dentist; it is outside the nurse's scope to refer independently.
whyNot.3: Treating it first could mask the lesion and delay referral.
